item.title: Azure Pipelines to publish Hugo blog on Github Pages
item.description: Keep the sources private in Azure Repos, host the site for free on GitHub Pages, and let a daily build publish scheduled posts on their day.
item.content:encoded:
Most tutorials about Hugo and GitHub Pages assume everything lives on GitHub and use GitHub Actions. My setup is a bit different:

  • the sources of the blog (Markdown, theme, config) live in a private Azure Repos repository;
  • the generated site is served by GitHub Pages, for free;
  • Azure Pipelines builds the site with Hugo and pushes the result to GitHub.

As a bonus, a daily run publishes posts that are written in advance: a post dated next Monday shows up on Monday, without touching anything.

Here is the whole setup, and the traps I fell into.

How it works

  1. I push a new post to the master branch of the Azure Repos repository.
  2. Azure Pipelines starts, installs Hugo and builds the site into public/.
  3. The pipeline copies public/ into the GitHub Pages repository and pushes it.
  4. GitHub Pages serves the new version a minute later.

On top of that, the pipeline also runs every day at a fixed time, so posts with a date in the future are published on their day.

What you need

  • A Hugo site in an Azure Repos repository (here the theme is a git submodule in themes/).
  • A GitHub Pages repository, for example <github-user>/<github-user>.github.io, served from its master branch.
  • An Azure DevOps project where you can create pipelines.

A token that can only do one thing

The pipeline needs to push to the GitHub Pages repository. Don't use your password or a classic token with access to everything: create a fine-grained personal access token, in GitHub Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens:

  • Repository access: Only select repositories → the GitHub Pages repository only.
  • Permissions: Contents → Read and write. Nothing else.

Then store it in the pipeline: Edit → Variables → New variable, name it GITHUB_PAT, paste the token and tick Keep this value secret. A secret variable is masked in the logs and is not passed to scripts unless you map it explicitly (see the last step below).

Warning

Fine-grained tokens expire. Put a reminder in your calendar a few days before the end date: when the token expires, the build still succeeds but publishing fails.

The pipeline

Create azure-pipelines.yml at the root of the repository:

trigger:
  branches:
    include: [ master ]

# Daily build: posts dated today get published even without a new commit
schedules:
- cron: '0 10 * * *'        # always UTC
  displayName: Daily publish
  branches:
    include: [ master ]
  always: true              # run even if nothing changed in the repository

pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-latest

variables:
  HUGO_VERSION: '0.169.0'
  PAGES_REPO: 'github.com/<github-user>/<github-user>.github.io.git'
  PAGES_BRANCH: 'master'

steps:
- checkout: self
  fetchDepth: 0
  submodules: true          # the theme is a git submodule

- script: |
    set -e
    wget -q https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/releases/download/v$(HUGO_VERSION)/hugo_extended_$(HUGO_VERSION)_linux-amd64.tar.gz
    tar -xzf hugo_extended_$(HUGO_VERSION)_linux-amd64.tar.gz hugo
    sudo mv hugo /usr/local/bin/
    hugo version
  displayName: Install Hugo

- script: hugo --minify --cleanDestinationDir
  displayName: Build site

- script: |
    set -e
    git clone --depth 1 --branch $(PAGES_BRANCH) https://x-access-token:${GITHUB_PAT}@$(PAGES_REPO) pages
    find pages -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -name .git -exec rm -rf {} +
    cp -r public/. pages/
    touch pages/.nojekyll
    cd pages
    git config user.name "Azure Pipelines"
    git config user.email "azure-pipelines@users.noreply.github.com"
    git add -A
    if git diff --cached --quiet; then
      echo "No change to publish"
    else
      git commit -m "Publish $(Build.SourceVersion)"
      git push origin $(PAGES_BRANCH)
    fi
  displayName: Publish to GitHub Pages
  env:
    GITHUB_PAT: $(GITHUB_PAT)

Then in Azure DevOps: Pipelines → New pipeline → Azure Repos Git → your repository → Existing Azure Pipelines YAML file → /azure-pipelines.yml.

Step by step

Checkout. submodules: true fetches the theme, fetchDepth: 0 fetches the full history (useful if you ever enable Hugo's Git info for "last modified" dates).

Install Hugo. The version is pinned in a variable. Use the same version as on your machine, and take the extended build: most themes need it for SCSS. When you update Hugo locally, update this line too.

Build. --minify makes the HTML and CSS smaller, --cleanDestinationDir removes files of pages that no longer exist.

Publish. Instead of force-pushing a fresh repository every time, the step clones the GitHub Pages repository, replaces its content with the new site and commits only if something changed. The history of the published site stays readable, and the daily runs where nothing changed create no empty commit. .nojekyll tells GitHub Pages to serve the files as they are, without running Jekyll on them.

Note

The token reaches the script only because of the env: block at the end. Without it, ${GITHUB_PAT} is empty: secret variables are never exposed to scripts automatically.

Scheduled posts

This part needs no plugin: it's Hugo's default behaviour. A page whose date is in the future is not built (unless you run Hugo with --buildFuture). So:

---
title: "My next post"
date: 2026-12-01
draft: false
---

This post is pushed today, but it stays invisible until the first build on December 1st. That's the job of the schedules block: with always: true, the pipeline runs every day even when the repository didn't change, and Hugo picks up the posts whose day has come.

Tip

To preview a scheduled post on your machine, run hugo server --buildFuture.

Two details about the cron:

  • It is always in UTC. 0 10 * * * is 11:00 in Central Europe in winter and 12:00 in summer. There is no time zone option, so pick the hour that suits you best for both seasons, or use two schedules limited to their months.
  • After a push, check Pipelines → your pipeline → ⋮ → Scheduled runs: the next planned runs should be listed there.

The traps I fell into

fetch-depth is GitHub Actions syntax. My first run failed with Unexpected value 'fetch-depth'. In Azure Pipelines the checkout option is camelCase: fetchDepth.

The theme folder was empty. With the theme as a git submodule, the checkout doesn't fetch it unless you add submodules: true. Hugo then builds pages without any layout.

"Scheduled runs" was nowhere to be found. That menu only exists for YAML pipelines. And if a schedule was ever defined in the pipeline settings (Edit → ⋮ → Triggers), it overrides the one in the YAML: leave that tab empty.

The custom domain disappeared after a deployment. GitHub Pages stores the custom domain in a CNAME file at the root of the published repository. Since the pipeline replaces all the files, put CNAME in Hugo's static/ folder: it's copied into public/ at every build.

www.example.com

An old classic pipeline was still active. If you move from a classic (designer) pipeline to YAML, disable the old one, otherwise both run on each push.

When to use GitHub Actions instead

If your sources can live on GitHub, GitHub Actions is simpler: Pages can be deployed directly from a workflow, without a token or a second repository. This Azure Pipelines setup makes sense when you want the sources to stay private in Azure DevOps while keeping the free hosting of GitHub Pages, or when your other projects already run on Azure DevOps.

item.title: Teaching my robot vacuum some manners: presence-based vacuuming with Home Assistant
item.description: How I made my robot vacuum clean once a day, only when nobody is home, and politely step aside when someone comes back, using Home Assistant, zone.home and four small automations.
item.content:encoded:
A robot vacuum is great until it decides to clean the living room right when you sit down with a coffee. I wanted mine to follow a few simple house rules:

  • Clean once a day.
  • Only when nobody is home.
  • Only during the day, between 10:00 and 18:00.
  • If someone comes back mid-run, pause. If they leave again quickly, resume. If they stay, go back to the dock and try again at the next opportunity.

Here is how I built it in Home Assistant with one helper and four automations.

What you need

  • Home Assistant with your robot vacuum integrated. In the examples it is vacuum.robot_vacuum: replace it with your own entity ID. Any vacuum entity works, whatever the brand.
  • Presence detection for everyone in the house. I use the Home Assistant Companion app on each phone.
  • Each phone's device_tracker assigned to a Person (Settings → People → Track devices).

That last point matters. It powers the entity this whole setup depends on: zone.home.

Why zone.home instead of a group

My first version used an old-school group of phone trackers:

phone_group:
  name: PhoneGroup
  entities:
    - device_tracker.phone_1
    - device_tracker.phone_2
    - device_tracker.phone_3

A group of trackers is home when at least one member is home and not_home otherwise. It works, but there is a cleaner built-in option.

zone.home's state is the number of people currently at home. No group to maintain: add a person, and they are counted automatically. "Nobody is home" becomes zone.home < 1, and "someone is home" becomes zone.home > 0.

Since the state is a number, the right tool is a numeric_state trigger or condition, not a state one. More on that in the gotchas section.

Step 1: a "cleaned today" flag

I need to remember whether the vacuum already cleaned today. That's a job for an input_boolean. You can create it in the UI (Settings → Devices & services → Helpers → Create helper → Toggle) or in configuration.yaml:

input_boolean:
  vacuum_cleaned_today:
    name: "Vacuum cleaned today"
    icon: mdi:robot-vacuum

Watch out: no - under the helper ID. I first wrote - name: ..., which turns the properties into a list. Home Assistant rejected the whole helper with "expected a mapping for dictionary value", and my automations then complained about an unknown entity. The - is for lists of things (triggers, actions, group members), not for describing a single object.

Step 2: the four automations

All four go into automations.yaml as-is, or into the UI editor one at a time via ⋮ → Edit in YAML (drop the leading - ). They use the current syntax: triggers / conditions / actions, trigger: instead of platform:, and action: instead of service:.

1. Start when nobody is home

- id: vacuum_start_when_away
  alias: "Vacuum - Start when nobody is home"
  mode: single
  triggers:
    # 5 minutes after the last person leaves
    - trigger: numeric_state
      entity_id: zone.home
      below: 1
      for: "00:05:00"
    # everyone already left before 10:00
    - trigger: time
      at: "10:00:00"
  conditions:
    - condition: time
      after: "10:00:00"
      before: "18:00:00"
    - condition: numeric_state
      entity_id: zone.home
      below: 1
    - condition: state
      entity_id: input_boolean.vacuum_cleaned_today
      state: "off"
    - condition: state
      entity_id: vacuum.robot_vacuum
      # some models report "idle" on the dock, see the gotchas below
      state: "docked"
  actions:
    - action: vacuum.start
      target:
        entity_id: vacuum.robot_vacuum

There are two triggers because there are two ways to end up "home empty, during the cleaning window":

  • Everyone leaves during the window. The first trigger fires after 5 minutes of an empty house. The delay keeps a phone that briefly drops off Wi-Fi from launching a run.
  • Everyone left before 10:00. Nothing changes at 10:00, so the second trigger re-checks at the start of the window.

The conditions then make sure that the time is right, the house is still empty, the vacuum hasn't run today and it is sitting on its dock.

2. Mark today as done

- id: vacuum_mark_cleaned_today
  alias: "Vacuum - Mark today's cleaning"
  mode: single
  triggers:
    # any start, automatic or manual
    - trigger: state
      entity_id: vacuum.robot_vacuum
      to: "cleaning"
  actions:
    - action: input_boolean.turn_on
      target:
        entity_id: input_boolean.vacuum_cleaned_today

I deliberately trigger on the vacuum's state rather than setting the flag in automation #1. This way a run started from the manufacturer's app or the button on the robot also counts.

3. Pause when someone comes home

This is the most interesting one.

- id: vacuum_pause_on_return
  alias: "Vacuum - Pause when someone comes home"
  mode: single
  triggers:
    - trigger: numeric_state
      entity_id: zone.home
      above: 0
  conditions:
    - condition: state
      entity_id: vacuum.robot_vacuum
      state: "cleaning"
  actions:
    - action: vacuum.pause
      target:
        entity_id: vacuum.robot_vacuum
    - wait_for_trigger:
        - trigger: numeric_state
          entity_id: zone.home
          below: 1
      timeout: "00:10:00"
    - choose:
        # still someone home after 10 minutes: back to the dock
        - conditions: "{{ wait.trigger is none }}"
          sequence:
            - action: vacuum.return_to_base
              target:
                entity_id: vacuum.robot_vacuum
            # not finished: it will try again at the next absence (10:00-18:00)
            - action: input_boolean.turn_off
              target:
                entity_id: input_boolean.vacuum_cleaned_today
      # nobody home again: resume
      default:
        - action: vacuum.start
          target:
            entity_id: vacuum.robot_vacuum

When the first person arrives, the vacuum pauses immediately, then the automation waits up to 10 minutes:

  • The house empties again (someone just popped in to grab their keys): wait.trigger is set, so we fall through to default and resume cleaning.
  • The timeout expires (wait.trigger is none): someone is staying. The vacuum goes back to its dock and I reset the "cleaned today" flag. That run doesn't count, so automation #1 can start a fresh one at the next absence within the window.

4. Reset at midnight

- id: vacuum_reset_at_midnight
  alias: "Vacuum - Reset at midnight"
  mode: single
  triggers:
    - trigger: time
      at: "00:00:00"
  actions:
    - action: input_boolean.turn_off
      target:
        entity_id: input_boolean.vacuum_cleaned_today

New day, new chance to clean.

How it plays out

Situation What the vacuum does
Last person leaves at 11:30 Starts at 11:35
Everyone left at 8:00 Starts at 10:00
Last person leaves at 19:00 Nothing, outside the window
Someone comes back for 3 minutes mid-run Pauses, then resumes
Someone comes back for good mid-run Pauses, docks after 10 min, retries at the next absence
Already cleaned today, house empties again Nothing
Started by hand from the app Counts as today's run

Gotchas I ran into

The UI won't offer 0 or 1 for zone.home. With a State trigger, the "From/To" dropdown only lists Unavailable and Unknown, because the state is a number and the UI can't list numbers in advance. Use a Numeric state trigger with Above / Below instead.

numeric_state is more robust than to: "0". A state trigger with to: "0" can also fire when Home Assistant starts and zone.home goes from unknown to 0, which looks like "everyone just left" when nobody did. A numeric_state trigger only fires when the value actually crosses the threshold. Note that "nobody home" is below: 1, not below: 0: the count can never go negative, so below: 0 never fires.

docked vs idle: check your robot's states. The state names depend on the integration and the model. A vacuum sitting on its dock may report idle instead of docked, and some never report docked at all. If yours does that, automation #1 will never start it. Check Developer tools → States while the robot is charging, and again while it is cleaning (cleaning is used in automations #2 and #3), then adapt the conditions to what your robot actually reports.

Give automations an id. Without it, automations written in automations.yaml can't be edited in the visual editor.

Validate before reloading. Developer tools → YAML → Check configuration catches indentation and structure errors and points to the exact file and line. Once it's green, reload Automations (and Input booleans) from the same page. No full restart needed.

Ideas for later

  • A notification when the run finishes, or when the vacuum gets stuck.
  • Skip days, for example a workday condition or a "guests" toggle.
  • Room-specific cleaning (kitchen every day, bedrooms twice a week), if the integration supports segments.

For now, my vacuum has learned the most important rule of shared living: do your chores when nobody's watching, and get out of the way when someone walks in.

item.title: Add the Xiaomi Air Purifier 3C in Jeedom
item.description: Extract the Xiaomi token with the cloud tokens extractor and control the Air Purifier 3C from Jeedom.
item.content:encoded:
The Xiaomi air purifier is a wifi device and to be able to use it in Jeedom you'll need to extract its token.

It's possible to extract the token by using an old version of the Mi-Home app or using various strange manipulations.

For me it never worked and by chance I found the Xiaomi Cloud tokens extractor.

Before to use it, you need to add your purifier in the Mi-Home app and then you can execute the "token_extractor.exe".

The tool will ask you to enter your Mi-Home login, your password and the server to use. The last information isn't mandatory and if omitted the tool will scan all countries and will list different information about your devices.

For the purifier we just need to get the token.

As I've the Xiaomi Home plugin in Jeedom I thought it would be easy to add my new toy but it never worked (the information returned by the commands were always empty).

After a few searches, I found the miiocli tool that can be installed on your Jeedom host (you'll be able to see a list of compatible devices on the Github page).

First connect via SSH to your Jeedom host and execute the following command to install the JQ tool (used to manipulate JSON structure)

sudo apt-get install jq -y

Then you can install the miiocli tool:

sudo apt-get install libffi-dev libssl-dev -y
sudo pip3 install python-miio

To be able to see what you can do with the Air Purifier 3C, you can type the help command and it will describe the options and commands you can use:

sudo miiocli airpurifiermb4 --ip [YourPurifierIP] --token [YourPurifierToken] --help

The parameter "airpurifiermb4" is the device type to use with the command and is linked to the Xiaomi Air Purifier 3C.

When you validate the previous command, you'll see all the commands available to control your purifier.

In the following screenshot, I added a new script in Jeedom to be able to control my device.

The first command is used to get a json with all the information from the purifier (power, air quality, ...) and then I save it in a file on my server (don't forget to set the IP of your purifier and its token).

The second command is used to query the json file and get the power value (enter the IP of your Jeedom host).

The third command is used to power on the purifier and so on...

As you understood the sample, you'll be able to add more commands to get the rest of the information and with a few click you'll have a widget to control your device and I'm sure most of you will have a better design.

item.title: Force HTTPS access in Apache
item.description: Redirect every HTTP request to HTTPS with a few rewrite rules in Apache's default virtual host.
item.content:encoded:
If you configured a certificate to access your Jeedom with HTTPS and you don't want to let the HTTP access available, you can change your Apache settings to redirect HTTP access to the HTTPS automatically.

You'll need to ssh on your Jeedom server and edit the following file:

nano /etc/apache2/sites-available/000-default.conf

The part we want to modify is the virtual host defined for the HTTP port (80)

<VirtualHost *:80>
        ServerAdmin webmaster@localhost
        DocumentRoot /var/www/html
        ErrorLog /var/www/html/log/http.error
</VirtualHost>

And we'll edit the file to rewrite the HTTP access to the HTTPS access

<VirtualHost *:80>
        ServerAdmin webmaster@localhost
        DocumentRoot /var/www/html

        RewriteEngine on
        RewriteCond %{SERVER_NAME} =My.JeedomDomain.com
        RewriteRule ^ https://%{SERVER_NAME}%{REQUEST_URI} [END,QSA,R=permanent]

        ErrorLog /var/www/html/log/http.error
</VirtualHost>

You need to replace the "My.JeedomDomain.com" by your actual domain name used to access your Jeedom from outside your network.

When it's done, you just need to enable the rewrite module and restart Apache:

a2enmod rewrite
systemctl restart apache2

item.title: Secure the access to your Jeedom with Certbot
item.description: Get a free Let's Encrypt certificate for Jeedom with Certbot, renewed automatically.
item.content:encoded:
A few days ago, I created a post on how to redirect the HTTPS external traffic to a Jeedom in a private network.

Everything will work but you'll see in your browser that the website isn't secure. The reason is that there is no certificate available on your webserver (on your Jeedom).

To generate, use and auto renew a certificate we'll use CertBot

Certbot is a free, open source software tool for automatically using Let’s Encrypt certificates on manually-administrated websites to enable HTTPS.

Certbot is made by the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), a 501(c)3 nonprofit based in San Francisco, CA, that defends digital privacy, free speech, and innovation.

First, open a SSH connection to your Jeedom.

Install snapd

sudo snap install core; sudo snap refresh core

Install Certbot

sudo snap install --classic certbot

Check if you can run the certbot command

sudo ln -s /snap/bin/certbot /usr/bin/certbot

To get a certificate and have certbot automatically change your Apache configuration to serve it and to turn on HTTPS access in a single step, use the following command:

sudo certbot --apache

The certbot comes with a cron to automatically renew your certificate. But if you want to check if the auto renewal is working, you can use this command:

sudo certbot renew --dry-run

If it completes without errors, your certificate will be renewed automatically.

Please note that your HTTP(80) and HTTPS(443) port must be opened or the auto renewal will not work.

Now you can try to access your Jeedom with the HTTPS url and you'll see that the browser will display that the connection is "secure".

As a wise man said once:

HTTPS & SSL doesn't mean "trust this." It means "this is private." You may be having a private conversation with Satan.

— Scott Hanselman (@shanselman) April 4, 2012

Please note that you'll need to change your Jeedom configuration to add the HTTPS URL (and port) to be able to use the HTTPS URL to access Jeedom.

item.title: Redirect HTTP/HTTPS port to your Jeedom
item.description: Forward HTTP and HTTPS from a Dream Machine Pro to the Jeedom box on your private network.
item.content:encoded:
In the previous blog post we saw how to create a custom domain name to point to our public IP address. The main goal was to be able to access our Jeedom from outside our private network.

But if you just type your public IP address or use the new custom domain name to access Jeedom you'll just hit your modem or firewall and they'll not know what do to with the traffic. And you can be sure the traffic will not go to your Jeedom by default.

If you're using a Dream Machine Pro (controller 6.2.26) you can redirect the HTTP/HTTPS traffic to your Jeedom by following these steps:

  1. Open your Dream Machine Network Manager web page
  2. Go to Advanced features - Advanced Gateway Settings and click on the Create a new Port Forwarding button
  3. Fill in the form as below and validate

You can repeat the process to redirect the HTTPS port (443).

Now if you enter your custom domain in a browser, you'll be able to access your Jeedom in your private network

item.title: Create a DynHost to access your Jeedom
item.description: Point an OVH DynHost domain name to your home IP address to reach Jeedom from outside.
item.content:encoded:
If you want to access your Jeedom from outside your private network, you can do it using your public IP address or using a custom domain name pointing to your public IP address (if the HTTP or HTTPS port is opened).

For me and maybe for you, it's easier to remember a custom domain name and I decided to go with one on OVH.

Now that I have my custom domain I would like to use it to access my Jeedom and trust me or not, I didn't know it was so simple.

Create a new user

Go in the DynHost menu and choose to create a username.

  • Enter a username suffix
  • Enter the sub-domain that you want to define to point to your Jeedom
  • Define a password to use with your username and confirm

Create a DynHostRecord

When it's done, you can add a new DynHost record and re-enter the sub-domain name you choosed earlier, enter the target IP (the public IP address of your Jeedom) and confirm.

If you want to know your public IP address you can go to whatismyipaddress and copy the address displayed in the IPv4 field.

In an upcoming blog post, we'll see how to automatically refresh your public IP address to DynHost (if you don't have a fixed IP address) and how to redirect incoming traffic on the HTTP port to your Jeedom.

item.title: CSS currentColor value
item.description: Define a color once and reuse it in borders, shadows and more with the CSS currentColor keyword.
item.content:encoded:
A few days ago, I started to learn CSS and HTML. I already played with CSS and HTML but I had a very very limited knowledge.

As I don't like to repeat a code or a property value, I found recently that you can apply a color (defined once) in different properties.

Let's see an example:

div {
    color: blue;
    border: 1px solid currentColor;
}

With the currentColor property you indicate that you'll use the value of the color property in other properties that accept a color value.

With my example, the border color will be blue.

You can even use it in a cascade:

body {
    color: blue;
}
div {
     border: 1px solid currentColor;
}

item.title: Update Jeedom from version 4.0.x to 4.1.x
item.description: Moving a Raspberry Pi Jeedom from 4.0 on Debian 9 to 4.1 on Debian 10, without losing anything.
item.content:encoded:
Well, Mr. Hunt, this is not Mission: Difficult, its Mission: Impossible. Difficult should be a walk in the park for you. - Boss, Mission: Impossible 2

Sometimes, a simple update is harder than you think. Since years, I've a Jeedom running on a Raspberry 3B+ and the last Jeedom update installed is the version 4.0.x hosted in a Debian 9 Stretch.

A few days ago I saw that the Jeedom 4.1.x was available with some really nice improvements.

The condition to be able to install this version is to have the Debian 10 Buster installed. As we can read in the install documentation, the best thing to do is to backup your Jeedom and install everything from scratch.

And that's what I did, downloaded the ISO x86, burned the SDCard, booted on it and installed Jeedom with the command line.

Right after that, I restored my Jeedom backup (I'll not describe that part here).

Now the fun part begins: Boot from the SSD.

When you check some websites, you'll read that you just need to install Debian on the SSD, plug it in the Raspberry and restart the device to boot from the SSD. But there are lies! (It was in my case)

The best thing I could find was to clone my SDCard to my SSD and it was really easy with the rpi-clone script.

rpi-clone is a shell script that is for cloning a running Raspberry Pi booted source disk (SD card or USB disk) to a destination disk which will be bootable. Destination disks are SD cards in the SD card slot or a USB card reader, USB flash disks, or USB hard drives.

First, clone the repository and copy the setup in your /usr/local/sbin directory:

git clone https://github.com/billw2/rpi-clone.git
cd rpi-clone
sudo cp rpi-clone rpi-clone-setup /usr/local/sbin

Stop the following services:

sudo service mysql stop
sudo service cron stop
sudo service apache2 stop
sudo service nginx stop

Connect your SSD to your Raspberry and clone your SDCard to your SSD:

rpi-clone sda -f

When it's done, you can restart the services:

sudo service mysql start
sudo service cron start
sudo service apache2 start

The next thing to do is to configure your Raspberry to be able to boot on the USB port. For that, you'll need to backup your current config.txt file, set the boot mode and then restart the Raspberry:

cp /boot/config.txt /boot/config.txt.old
echo program_usb_boot_mode=1 | sudo tee -a /boot/config.txt
sudo reboot

When your device restarted, you can check if the boot mode is set to boot on USB with the following command:

vcgencmd otp_dump | grep 17
>17:3020000a

If it returns 17:3020000a, the setting has been taken into account. Now we need to change the boot config to be able to boot on the SSD.

Get the PARTUUID from your SSD (/dev/sda2):

sudo blkid

Backup your current cmdline file:

sudo cp /boot/cmdline.txt /boot/cmdline.txt.bak

Edit the cmdline file and replace the PARTUUID with the value we copied from the sudo blkid command, save and quit:

sudo nano /boot/cmdline.txt

When it's done, you can reboot again:

sudo reboot

After the reboot, the following command should display the /dev/sda2 device:

findmnt -n -o SOURCE /
> /dev/sda2

Almost finished, now you need to change fstab to use the PARTUUID from your SSD device, save, quit and reboot again:

sudo nano /etc/fstab


sudo reboot

The next step is done to create a new partition on your SSD. As you'll see later, the partition size on your SSD is the same as your SDCard. Here we want to use the entire SSD disk size:

You'll need to reboot again when the partition is created. This time it may take a little longer.

It's not yet finished, now you need to resize the partition:

If everything went well, you should see the new partition size with the df command:

df -h

item.title: Refresh the Xiaomi door sensor status with a scenario in Jeedom
item.description: A Jeedom scenario that refreshes a Xiaomi door sensor that sometimes forgets its real state.
item.content:encoded:
Since the beginning I've never had an issue with my Xiaomi sensors but for no reason one of them started to not update his status.

If I close the door Jeedom still displays the door as opened.

I couldn't find the reason and I discovered that a simple refresh command could reset the status and display the right information.

If you don't want to refresh the status manually, you can do it with a scenario.

First, create a triggered scenario on the Xiaomi sensor for the opening command and give a name to your scenario.

Then in the scenario definition:

  1. add a Sleep action for 10 seconds
  2. add a refresh command from your Xiaomi sensor
  3. add an IF condition and check if the opening command value is equal to 1 (open)
  4. add a THEN condition to execute your current scenario

If the status changes, the scenario will wait 10 seconds and then execute the sensor refresh command. If the status is still equal to 1 (open), it will execute again the current scenario.

Now if the door is closed and the status is not up to date the scenario will update it after 10 seconds.

item.title: How to display device name in your Pi-hole
item.description: Show device names instead of IP addresses in Pi-hole with conditional forwarding.
item.content:encoded:
When your Pi-hole doesn't act as a DHCP server (because you already have another one) you'll able to see only the IP addresses of the devices.

Not really user-friendly when you need to analyze the log of the Pi-Hole.

But don't be afraid, there is a solution!

To be able to see the device name, you just need to enable the Use Conditional Forwarding setting in the Settings - DNS.

When the option is enabled, enter the local network to use and the IP address of your DHCP server as described in the screenshot, save and it's done. It's magic.

item.title: Accept DNS queries to specific IP addresses within your Dream Machine Pro
item.description: Firewall rules on a UniFi Dream Machine Pro so every DNS query goes through your Pi-hole and nowhere else.
item.content:encoded:
Holidays are nice when you want to try something new.
In my case, I wanted to install a Pi-Hole.
If you never heard about Pi-Hole, it's a DNS sinkhole that protects your devices from unwanted content, without installing any client-side software.

My post isn't a How-to install/configure/... the thing.
Here we'll see how to create firewall rules on the Dream Machine Pro to refuse all DNS queries except the one to the Pi-Hole.

The first thing to do is to create two groups in the firewall settings.

One to specify the DNS port to block (53) and another one to contain the IP addresses that will be used to accept DNS queries (The Pi-Hole address and maybe some other DNS addresses).

I use groups to be able to add/remove address or port as I wish.

First group

  • Name: DNS Port
  • Type: Port
  • Port value: 53

Second group

  • Name: DNS to Accept
  • Type: Address IPV4
  • Address: The address of your PI-Hole and maybe some other public DNS addresses

When it's done, we need to create two firewall rules. One to block all outbound traffic to the port 53 and another one to accept all outbound traffic to the port 53 but only for the addresses we trust.

First rule

  • Name: Accept DNS Group
  • Rule applied: Before predefined rules
  • Action: Accept
  • Source Type: Address/Port group
  • Source IPv4 Address Group: Any
  • Source Port Group: Any
  • Destination Type: Address/Port group
  • Destination IPv4 Address Group: DNS to Accept (the second group we created)
  • Destination Port Group: DNS Port (the first group we created)

Second rule

  • Name: Drop other DNS
  • Rule applied: Before predefined rules
  • Action: Drop
  • Source Type: Address/Port group
  • Source IPv4 Address Group: Any
  • Source Port Group: Any
  • Destination Type: Address/Port group
  • Destination IPv4 Address Group: Any
  • Destination Port Group: DNS Port (the first group we created)

With these rules, the devices connected to our LAN will only use the DNS we trust and if a malware tries to bypass our DNS, it will be blocked by the second firewall rule.

item.title: Change Proximus Internet password
item.description: Lost your Proximus PPPoE password? Set a new one from the MyProducts page, no old password needed.
item.content:encoded:
In some cases you'll handle the PPPoE connection in your router.
The main reason is to connect to the Proximus network from your router and let your personal hardware manage the DHCP.

If you know your login and password, it's really easy. But if like me, you lost your original password / don't remember it / never saved it in your favorite password tool / ... you're doomed. Or not.

Proximus made it simple, you can login on their website and in the MyProducts section you need to select your "Internet" product.
From there you'll be able to define a new password without the need to enter your old password.

When the password is changed, it will take effect within two hours.

My first error was to change it too in my modem -> No more Internet at home.
In fact you can use the old password as long as Proximus didn't validate your new password.

Two hours later... No Internet!

The WAF was aligned with the two hours but not with more.

I had two solutions:

  1. Try a new password on Proximus website (and wait two more hours)
  2. Contact the Support

I don't remember my web search but I found a ticket about the PPPoE connection with the Proximus modem and the new password rule.
In fact, the new password must be eight characters long and it must only contain alphanumeric characters.

The thing I didn't say is that I used a password generator to have something complex on my first try.

So before to call the Support, I changed my password to match the rule (on Proximus website and in my router) and it worked right away.

item.title: Change the status bar color in your Xamarin.Forms app
item.description: One line in styles.xml to change the Android status bar color of a Xamarin.Forms app.
item.content:encoded:
It's the second time I need to change the status bar color in a Xamarin.Forms (Android) and I didn't remember how to do it.

As I don't want to search it again, I decided to add the information here.

The status bar is the top part of the application where you can find the battery level, the network status,...

In your Android project, just add the following line in the styles.xml file and use the color you like:

<item name="android:statusBarColor">#3F4550</item>

item.title: Frame HeightRequest not applied
item.description: A Xamarin.Forms Frame ignores HeightRequest because of its default padding: set Padding to 0.
item.content:encoded:
For each of my items in the ListView, I wanted to display the title of the show and the remaining episodes.
But it can be really difficult to see the label on an image.

A solution I used in my previous Windows Phone app was to add a border with a background color. So I decided to use the same tip with the Frame control.

<Frame Grid.Row="0" HeightRequest="22" VerticalOptions="End"  BackgroundColor="#80000000" >
    <StackLayout Orientation="Horizontal">
        <Label Grid.Row="0"  Text="{Binding Title}" TextColor="#FFFFFF" Margin="5,0,0,0" LineBreakMode="TailTruncation" 
                    HorizontalOptions="StartAndExpand" FontAttributes="Bold" FontSize="Subtitle"/>
        <Label Grid.Row="0"  Text="{Binding User.Remaining}" TextColor="#FFFFFF" Margin="0,0,5,0" HorizontalOptions="End" 
                    FontAttributes="Bold" FontSize="Subtitle" />
    </StackLayout>
</Frame>

As you can see, the HeightRequest seems to be ignored. It's bigger than expected. In fact, the Frame control has a default padding of 20.

To have the expected result, you just need to set the Frame's Padding to 0.

<Frame Grid.Row="0" HeightRequest="22" VerticalOptions="End"  BackgroundColor="#80000000" Padding="0">
    <StackLayout Orientation="Horizontal">
        <Label Grid.Row="0"  Text="{Binding Title}" TextColor="#FFFFFF" Margin="5,0,0,0" LineBreakMode="TailTruncation" 
                    HorizontalOptions="StartAndExpand" FontAttributes="Bold" FontSize="Subtitle"/>
        <Label Grid.Row="0"  Text="{Binding User.Remaining}" TextColor="#FFFFFF" Margin="0,0,5,0" HorizontalOptions="End" 
                    FontAttributes="Bold" FontSize="Subtitle" />
    </StackLayout>
</Frame>

And now the HeightRequest defined is applied.

item.title: Syntax Highlighting In Wyam
item.description: Stop code blocks from wrapping on phones and let them scroll horizontally, with two CSS lines.
item.content:encoded:
In my previous blog post I saw that the syntax highlighting was weird on a phone.
A carriage return was added automatically instead of taking advantage of the power of a scrollbar.

To avoid the carriage return and let the scrollbar work as expected we need to override the CSS with the following style: 
pre code {
        white-space: pre;
        word-wrap: normal;
}

Just create the following folder structure in your input directory, create a file named override.css and add the pre code style in it.

Build your blog and start the preview to see the result.

item.title: Row height in ListView ItemTemplate
item.description: Grid row heights are ignored in a Xamarin.Forms ListView until you set HasUnevenRows to True.
item.content:encoded:
In my App I wanted to have a view for my TV shows.
As I have a WPF and Windows Phone background, I tried to set the row height on the Grid RowDefinition.

<ListView ItemsSource="{Binding Shows}" VerticalOptions="FillAndExpand" >
    <ListView.ItemTemplate>
        <DataTemplate>
            <ViewCell>
                <Grid>
                    <Grid.ColumnDefinitions>
                         <ColumnDefinition Width="*"/>
                    </Grid.ColumnDefinitions>
                    <Grid.RowDefinitions>								
                         <RowDefinition Height="100"/>
                    </Grid.RowDefinitions>
                    
                    <ffimageloading:CachedImage Grid.Row="0" Source="{Binding Image.Banner}"
                        Aspect="AspectFill"							
                        RetryCount= "3"
                        RetryDelay= "600"
                        HeightRequest="100"
                        DownsampleToViewSize = "true"	/>
                        
                    <Frame Grid.Row="0" HeightRequest="20" VerticalOptions="End" Padding="0"
                        BackgroundColor="#80000000" >
                        <StackLayout Orientation="Horizontal">
                            <Label Grid.Row="0"  Text="{Binding Title}" TextColor="#FFFFFF" Margin="5,0,0,0"
                            LineBreakMode="TailTruncation" HorizontalOptions="StartAndExpand"/>
                            <Label Grid.Row="0"  Text="{Binding User.Remaining}" TextColor="#FFFFFF"
                            Margin="0,0,5,0" HorizontalOptions="End"/>
                        </StackLayout>
                    </Frame>
                </Grid>
            </ViewCell>
        </DataTemplate>
    </ListView.ItemTemplate>
</ListView>

But the result was completely wrong. The black frame is too big and the show title is not displayed.

I tried to change the row definition of the Grid to Auto and let the image take the needed height but the result was the same.

In fact, you have to set the HasUnevenRows property of the ListView to True to force the row height otherwise the ListView will use his default row height size (and the behaviour will be really strange).

<ListView ItemsSource="{Binding Shows}"  VerticalOptions="FillAndExpand" HasUnevenRows="True" >

For iOS, I read that you have to set the RowHeight on the ListView or the size will be ignored. I couldn't verify the behaviour but since my items have the same height, I can set the RowHeight property on the ListView and remove the HasUnevenRows property to use its default value (False).

<ListView ItemsSource="{Binding Shows}"  VerticalOptions="FillAndExpand" RowHeight="100">

And here is the result:

item.title: A new adventure
item.description: The first post: why this blog exists and how it gets published.
item.content:encoded:
Yeah! The first post.
I really wanted to start my blog and I finally decided to install everything to do so.
Even if you only see a simple page, I had a fun time with my Azure Pipeline.
